expectedText:
SCHOOL ACTIVITIES LEAVE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

ABOUT SCHOOL ACTIVITIES LEAVE
This document addresses California Labor Code § 230.8, which protects an employee's job when the employee takes limited, unpaid or leave-bank time off for certain child-related school and licensed child care activities. This is a distinct, narrow statutory protection — it does not replace, and is not the same as, the California Family Rights Act (CFRA), Pregnancy Disability Leave, Paid Family Leave, bereavement leave, kin care, jury duty or witness leave, domestic violence leave, or reproductive loss leave, each of which is a separate leave entitlement governed by its own statute. A related but separate statute, Labor Code § 230.7, protects an employee who takes time off to appear at a child's school in response to a request made under Education Code § 48900.1 (a suspension-related school appearance); that separate statute is not addressed in this document.

Employee: Jordan Lee
Employer: Acme, Inc.
Child: Riley Lee
Employee's relationship to child: Maternal aunt

WHICH EMPLOYERS ARE COVERED
Labor Code § 230.8 applies only to an employer that employs 25 or more employees working at the same location. A covered employer may not discharge or in any way discriminate against an employee who is a parent of one or more children of the age to attend kindergarten or grades 1 to 12, or a licensed child care provider, for taking off up to 40 hours each year for the child-related activities the statute describes.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "An employer who employs 25 or more employees working at the same location shall not discharge or in any way discriminate against an employee who is a parent of one or more children of the age to attend kindergarten or grades 1 to 12, inclusive, or a licensed child care provider, for taking off up to 40 hours each year, for the purpose of either of the following child-related activities:"
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 230.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Lab. Code § 230.8(a)(1), employer coverage threshold and core prohibition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=230.8.)
  Known gap: The statute does not define "the same location," and does not say how an employer with employees spread across multiple sites, or an employee who works at more than one site, is measured against the 25-employee threshold. This 25-or-more-employees-at-the-same-location coverage threshold is a real limit on who this law protects — it is not a companywide headcount test, and an employee at a smaller location may fall outside this particular statute even if the employer is large overall.

WHAT TIME OFF IS COVERED
The statute covers two distinct categories of child-related activities, within an overall cap of up to 40 hours in a year. The first category is finding, enrolling, or reenrolling a child in a school or with a licensed child care provider, or participating in activities of the child's school or licensed child care provider, after the employee gives the employer reasonable notice of the planned absence in advance; time off in this first category cannot exceed eight hours in any calendar month. The second category is addressing a "child care provider or school emergency," a defined term covering situations such as the school or provider requesting the child be picked up or excluding the child under an attendance policy, behavioral or discipline problems, closure or unexpected unavailability of the school or provider, or a natural disaster, after the employee gives the employer notice.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "To find, enroll, or reenroll his or her child in a school or with a licensed child care provider, or to participate in activities of the school or licensed child care provider of his or her child, if the employee, prior to taking the time off, gives reasonable notice to the employer of the planned absence of the employee. Time off pursuant to this subparagraph shall not exceed eight hours in any calendar month of the year."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 230.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Lab. Code § 230.8(a)(1)(A), finding/enrolling/participating category and its monthly cap (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=230.8.)
  "To address a child care provider or school emergency, if the employee gives notice to the employer."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 230.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Lab. Code § 230.8(a)(1)(B), child care provider or school emergency category (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=230.8.)
  "“Child care provider or school emergency” means that an employee’s child cannot remain in a school or with a child care provider due to one of the following:"
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 230.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Lab. Code § 230.8(e)(2), definition of “child care provider or school emergency” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=230.8.)
  Known gap: The statute's opening 40-hours-per-year cap applies to both categories of activity together, but the additional eight-hours-per-calendar-month sub-cap is written to apply only to the first category (finding, enrolling, or participating) — the statute does not say the emergency-pickup category is separately capped at eight hours a month. The statute also does not state a minimum amount of advance notice that counts as "reasonable" for the first category, and, for the emergency category, only requires that the employee "gives notice," without using the word "reasonable." No case law interpreting these terms is cited in this document; a CourtListener case-law search for this statute was not completed because the research session's daily case-law search quota was already exhausted, so this document is limited to the statutory text.

WHO COUNTS AS A "PARENT" AND PRIORITY BETWEEN TWO PARENTS
For purposes of this statute, "parent" is defined broadly: a parent, guardian, stepparent, foster parent, or grandparent of a child, or a person who stands in loco parentis to a child. Where more than one parent of the same child is employed by the same employer at the same worksite, the entitlement to take a planned absence as to that child belongs, at any one time, only to whichever parent first gives the employer notice; the other parent may take a simultaneous planned absence for that same child only with the employer's approval.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Parent” means a parent, guardian, stepparent, foster parent, or grandparent of, or a person who stands in loco parentis to, a child."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 230.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Lab. Code § 230.8(e)(1), definition of “parent” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=230.8.)
  "If more than one parent of a child is employed by the same employer at the same worksite, the entitlement under paragraph (1) of a planned absence as to that child applies, at any one time, only to the parent who first gives notice to the employer, such that another parent may take a planned absence simultaneously as to that same child under the conditions described in paragraph (1) only if he or she obtains the employer’s approval for the requested time off."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 230.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Lab. Code § 230.8(a)(2), priority between two parents employed by the same employer (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=230.8.)
  Known gap: The current text of this statute defines eligibility by this list of family relationships and by the child being of an age to attend kindergarten through grade 12, or by the employee being a licensed child care provider — it does not use a separate "custody" test, and it does not single out grandparents as needing to have custody of the child to qualify. This document is based on the statute as currently in effect; it does not trace the legislative history of this eligible-relationship list or confirm it has not changed since this text was last amended.

NOTICE, AND WHETHER THE TIME OFF IS PAID
This leave is not automatically paid on top of an employee's other leave banks: the employee must use existing vacation, personal leave, or compensatory time off for the planned absence, unless a collective bargaining agreement entered into before January 1, 1995 and still in effect provides otherwise; an employee may also use unpaid time for this purpose to the extent the employer makes that available. If all of an employer's permanent, full-time employees are given vacation during the same period of the year, an employee may not use accrued vacation at any other time of year for this purpose.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The employee shall utilize existing vacation, personal leave, or compensatory time off for purposes of the planned absence authorized by this section, unless otherwise provided by a collective bargaining agreement entered into before January 1, 1995, and in effect on that date. An employee also may utilize time off without pay for this purpose, to the extent made available by his or her employer."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 230.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Lab. Code § 230.8(b)(1), use of existing leave banks or unpaid time (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=230.8.)
  "Notwithstanding paragraph (1), in the event that all permanent, full-time employees of an employer are accorded vacation during the same period of time in the calendar year, an employee of that employer may not utilize that accrued vacation benefit at any other time for purposes of the planned absence authorized by this section."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 230.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Lab. Code § 230.8(b)(2), companywide-vacation-period limitation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=230.8.)
  Known gap: The statute does not create a separate, additional paid-leave bank for this purpose — it directs the employee to an existing vacation, personal leave, or compensatory time balance (or unpaid time, if the employer makes that available), so how much paid time off is actually available depends on the employee's own accrued balances and the employer's own unpaid-time practices, not on this statute alone. The statute also says an employee's entitlement under this section cannot be diminished by a collective bargaining agreement term agreed to on or after January 1, 1995, a detail this document does not further develop.

DOCUMENTATION THE EMPLOYER MAY REQUEST
If the employer requests it, the employee must provide documentation from the school or licensed child care provider showing that the employee engaged in the covered child-related activity on a specific date and at a particular time. The statute defines "documentation" as whatever written verification of parental participation the school or licensed child care provider itself deems appropriate and reasonable.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The employee, if requested by the employer, shall provide documentation from the school or licensed child care provider as proof that he or she engaged in child-related activities permitted in subdivision (a) on a specific date and at a particular time. For purposes of this subdivision, “documentation” means whatever written verification of parental participation the school or licensed child care provider deems appropriate and reasonable."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 230.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Lab. Code § 230.8(c), documentation the employer may require (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=230.8.)
  Known gap: The statute leaves the content and format of acceptable "documentation" to what the school or child care provider itself deems appropriate and reasonable — it does not specify a required form, and different schools or providers may verify participation differently. The documentation requirement is worded as proof of having "engaged in child-related activities permitted in subdivision (a)" generally; this document does not resolve whether, or how, that requirement is meant to apply to the emergency-pickup category as distinct from the finding/enrolling/participating category.

ANTI-DISCRIMINATION PROTECTION AND REMEDIES
An employee who is discharged, threatened with discharge, demoted, suspended, or otherwise discriminated against in the terms and conditions of employment because the employee took time off for a covered child-related activity is entitled to reinstatement and reimbursement of lost wages and work benefits caused by the employer's acts. If an employer willfully refuses to rehire, promote, or otherwise restore an employee or former employee who has been determined eligible for rehiring or promotion through a grievance procedure, arbitration, or hearing authorized by law, the employer is subject to a civil penalty equal to three times the amount of the employee's lost wages and work benefits.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Any employee who is discharged, threatened with discharge, demoted, suspended, or in any other manner discriminated against in terms and conditions of employment by his or her employer because the employee has taken time off to engage in child-related activities permitted in subdivision (a) shall be entitled to reinstatement and reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits caused by the acts of the employer. Any employer who willfully refuses to rehire, promote, or otherwise restore an employee or former employee who has been determined to be eligible for rehiring or promotion by a grievance procedure, arbitration, or hearing authorized by law shall be subject to a civil penalty in an amount equal to three times the amount of the employee’s lost wages and work benefits."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 230.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Lab. Code § 230.8(d), prohibition on retaliation and available remedies (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=230.8.)
  Known gap: The statute itself does not name a specific agency or set a specific filing deadline for pursuing these remedies, and no case law construing this remedy provision is cited here: a CourtListener case-law search for this statute returned a 429 daily-quota-exceeded error before any results could be reviewed, so this document relies on the statutory text alone rather than waiting out or retrying that quota.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Please sign below to acknowledge review of this School Activities Leave information sheet.

Employee: Jordan Lee
Employer: Acme, Inc.
Date: September 1, 2026
